name: Ben Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a big hydraulic excavator at an open-cut coal mine, the kind with a bucket you could park a car in. I'm on the overburden mostly, that's the dirt and rock on top of the coal, and I load trucks all shift. It starts with a prestart, a walk around, greasing, then I'm digging by quarter past seven and I don't stop much till crib. What I like is getting a good rhythm with the truck drivers so nobody waits, and what wears me out is the night roster, three nights on, and the way it messes with the kids' weekends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use AI tools. Where do they fit into your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly outside the cab. I use a chatbot on my phone at crib to explain the fleet reports they hand out, because half of it's written for engineers. I've also been using it to study for an electrical course I started at night, it's a good patient teacher at eleven at night when nobody else is. My mates think I'm a bit of a nerd about it, Tomasz calls me the professor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, see, it's a tool, not a tidal wave, and that's fine. I'd probably post something like that, because I've been one of the people saying it's useful. At work I'd tell the guys they can stop worrying and start using it for the boring stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, really, because the bigger thing for us was never AI. This mine's got a closure date in the 2030s anyway, because of the move away from coal. So I was always going to need a plan B, AI just made it more urgent in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the electrical course at night, that's about two more years. I'd keep using the chatbot to study and maybe show a couple of the guys how to use it on the reports. Money-wise, nothing changes, we put away about two hundred a fortnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, but I was already moving, so it's not a big change in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the mine has a closure date anyway. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed, honestly. I vote for the climate stuff, I want the kids to have a decent planet, and I know that means places like this close. But I also know what it does to a town when a mine goes. I'd rather we did it properly than pretended it wasn't coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the guys about the chatbot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to ask it what the numbers on the fleet report actually mean, like why our cycle times were slow last week. Tomasz would roll his eyes for about a day and then he'd be asking me how to get it to write his kid's birthday poem. That's usually how it goes with him.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a tool, not a tidal wave, and that's fine. I'd tell the guys at work they can stop worrying and use it for the boring stuff.
S0.think: It changes nothing for me, because the mine has a closure date in the 2030s anyway. I always needed a plan B, and AI just made that feel more urgent.
S0.do: Keeps going with his two-year night electrical course and shows a few workmates how to use a chatbot on the fleet reports. Keeps saving about two hundred a fortnight.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit relieved, since he was already moving.
S0.quote: Tomasz would roll his eyes for about a day and then he'd be asking me how to get it to write his kid's birthday poem.
S0.fieldNote: Ben's real horizon is the coal mine's closure, not AI, and he's already acting on it. His progressive politics show in his mixed but accepting view of the energy transition. He casts himself as the person who helps workmates use new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time for the union to get ahead of it, not fight it. Workers should get trained on the company's dime and share in what the machines save. I'd probably be the one at the union meeting saying, let's write the training into the agreement now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's not bad at all, honestly. I'm already halfway to an electrician's ticket, and someone's going to have to wire and fix all these new machines. What bothers me is the blokes who aren't moving, because they'll be the ones left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the electrical course faster if I could, maybe drop a night shift a month and do more study. I'd ask the company if they'd let me do my practical hours on their maintenance crew. And I'd run a little session at crib for anyone who wants to learn the AI stuff, no charge, just sandwiches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually, with a bit of worry for the others. It feels like the thing I've been preparing for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Dropping a night shift costs money. What would that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three hundred a fortnight less, roughly. Ana's a planner at the council so she's on a steady wage, and we'd cut the streaming and the takeaways and that'd cover most of it. She's always been the one saying, go for it, so she'd back me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, funnily enough. He's brilliant on a machine but he left school at fifteen and he hates anything with a screen. I'd want to drag him along to my crib sessions, but you can't make a man learn.

S1.say: I'd say the union should get ahead of the change, not fight it. Workers should be trained at the company's cost and share in what the machines save.
S1.think: It's not bad for me, because I'm already halfway to an electrician's ticket and someone has to wire and fix the new machines. What bothers me is the workmates who aren't moving.
S1.do: Drops a night shift a month to speed up his electrical course and asks to do practical hours on the company maintenance crew. Runs free crib-time sessions teaching AI tools and trims household spending to cover lost pay.
S1.feel: Pretty good, as if this is what he's been preparing for, with some worry for others.
S1.quote: I'd run a little session at crib for anyone who wants to learn the AI stuff, no charge, just sandwiches.
S1.fieldNote: Ben feels ready for this picture and his mood stays calm, which follows from a plan he already started. He's willing to take a pay cut to move faster. His worry is collective rather than personal, centred on mates like Tomasz.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a universal basic income, a payment everyone gets whether they work or not, and I'd say it loudly. If machines do all the work, the money they make has to come back to people. I'd be posting about it, writing to politicians, the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my electrician plan goes out the window, because robots that can mine can also wire a switchboard. I'm not much better off than the guys who did nothing, I just have a nicer certificate. That's a hard thing to admit after all those late nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the course if it really looked like that, and put the energy into earning and saving while the job's still there, every overtime shift going. I'd get involved in a campaign for basic income, actually join something, not just like posts. And I'd look at whether jobs in setting up and fixing robots exist yet, because for a year or two someone will be doing that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit gutted. Not hopeless, because I think it could actually be good if we share it, but scared we won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change for you, compared with ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years you jump on whatever's moving right now, there's no time to plan a career. With ten I could finish my ticket, work on the robot side, and probably see it coming. With two I'm basically making it up month by month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it could be good if it's shared. What would good look like for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana and I both home more, the kids not caught up in our rosters. Jonah's thirteen and he'd love it if I was at his games. But that only works if the money still comes in, and right now nobody's promising that.

S2.say: I'd say loudly that this is the moment for a universal basic income. If machines do all the work, the money they make has to come back to people.
S2.think: My electrician plan goes out the window, because robots that can mine can also wire a switchboard. I'm not much better off than people who did nothing, which is hard to admit.
S2.do: Pauses his course and works every overtime shift to save while the job lasts. Joins a basic income campaign and looks for short-term work setting up and fixing robots.
S2.feel: Anxious and a bit gutted, but hopeful the change could be good if it's shared.
S2.quote: I'm not much better off than the guys who did nothing, I just have a nicer certificate.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture knocks out Ben's plan, and he says so honestly. He stays anxious rather than alarmed because he's comfortable with risk and sees a possible upside. His politics turn quickly into joining an actual campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up a basic income and pay for it with a tax on the profits from robots. I'd say it at the union and online, and I'd be specific about it. We know what's coming, so build the safety net now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is just enough to get one more good run. I'd finish the electrical course and go straight into robot maintenance, because for a few years that's where the work will be. After that, I don't know, and I'd rather say I don't know than pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the course in the next eighteen months and apply for any job working on the automated fleet, even at the mine down the road. I'd use the AI tools to learn the robot side now, the manuals, the fault codes. I'd keep two hundred a fortnight going into savings and add whatever extra overtime I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More like a puzzle than a threat, which is how I like problems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a robot maintenance job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a few years, yes, I'd do a fly-in fly-out roster if I had to, two weeks on and one off. Ana would hate it, and I'd miss the kids, but it'd be for a set time with a goal. We'd talk it through first, she gets a vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between the five-year and two-year pictures for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In five, my plan still works, it just has an end date. In two, it doesn't work at all. Three years doesn't sound like much, but it's the difference between finishing the course and throwing it away.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to set up a basic income paid for by a tax on robot profits. We know it's coming, so we should build the safety net now.
S3.think: Five years gives me one more good run: finish the electrical course and work on robot maintenance. After that I honestly don't know.
S3.do: Finishes his course in about eighteen months and applies for automated-fleet maintenance jobs, even at another mine. Uses AI tools to study robot manuals and fault codes and keeps saving, adding overtime.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but treating it more like a puzzle than a threat.
S3.quote: Three years doesn't sound like much, but it's the difference between finishing the course and throwing it away.
S3.fieldNote: Ben sees time very concretely as the gap between a finished and a wasted course. He's willing to take a fly-in fly-out roster for a few years, but makes it a family decision. He's honest about not knowing what comes after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, so let's do it right: training, a basic income, and a say for workers. I'd want our town to have a real plan, written down, by next year. I'd be the bloke at the council meeting with a printout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years suits me fine for my own work, I'd get through the robot maintenance years and probably into something running them. What I really think about is the kids, because Jonah would be twenty-three in the world it ends up in. I want him to have a reason to get up in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my electrical ticket and get into robot maintenance within three years. I'd help set up a transition group in town with the union and the council. And Ana and I would start talking to Jonah now about what he likes, not what pays, because pay might mean something different by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It feels like a big job ahead, not a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the kids need a reason to get up. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad got laid off from the steelworks when I was twelve and he spent two years on the couch. It wasn't the money, we got by, it was that he didn't know who he was. I don't want that for me or for Jonah.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been hopeful in most of the pictures. Is there anything in this one that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That ten years gives people an excuse to put it off. Governments love a deadline that's after the next election. If we waste eight of the ten years, we're back in the two-year picture, just later.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to do this right, with training, a basic income and a say for workers. I'd push for a written town plan by next year.
S4.think: Ten years suits my own work, through robot maintenance and maybe into running them. What I really think about is my son, who'd be twenty-three, and whether he'll have a reason to get up.
S4.do: Finishes his electrical ticket and moves into robot maintenance within three years. Helps start a town transition group with the union and council and talks to his son about interests over pay.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, like a big job ahead rather than a wall.
S4.quote: If we waste eight of the ten years, we're back in the two-year picture, just later.
S4.fieldNote: The story about his father on the couch explains much of Ben's drive and his focus on purpose, not just money. His main worry is that politicians will waste the time. He blends personal planning with community organising.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because everything I've been working on gets wiped out. What would help is a basic income that's ready before it lands, and training that's quick and paid, not a two-year course. Also honest information from the companies about which jobs go when.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about meaning. Everyone talks about money, and money matters, but I watched what losing work did to my dad. If the robots do everything, we need something for people to be proud of.

headlineQuote: It wasn't the money, we got by, it was that he didn't know who he was.
portrait: Ben Santos is a 43-year-old excavator operator at an open-cut coal mine that was already due to close in the 2030s, so he started a night electrical course before AI came into it. He uses AI tools every day to study and to read the mine's reports, and he likes teaching his workmates. He stays calm in the milder pictures and becomes anxious only when two-year AGI wipes out his plan. With more time he'd move into robot maintenance and help organise his town, driven by memories of his father's lost sense of purpose after a layoff.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it wipes out the electrical training he's been working towards.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income that's ready before AGI lands, quick paid training, and honest information from companies about which jobs go when.
